cues.text: A Marriage in Trouble
According to the traditional account, dated by the Church's own exhibition of recognized Eucharistic miracles to 1247 , a woman of Santarém believed her husband had been repeatedly unfaithful.
A local sorceress told her that a stolen consecrated Host, brought for use in a spell, would restore his affection.
A separate, more detailed record commissioned a century later by King Afonso IV instead dates the same events to 1266, a discrepancy later chroniclers have never fully resolved.
Carried From the Altar
At Mass in the Church of St. Stephen , the woman received the Host on her tongue as instructed.
She removed it, wrapped it in her veil, and hurried from the church before it could be consumed.
The linen began bleeding so visibly, before she had gone more than a few steps, that concerned parishioners assumed she had injured her own hand.
A Light From the Chest
Frightened by what she had done, the woman ran home and hid the bleeding Host, still wrapped in its veil, inside a wooden chest.
That night, she and her husband were woken by a brilliant light streaming from the chest itself.
By their own later account, they felt themselves in the presence of adoring angels as they knelt before it until dawn.
Confession and a Second Sign
At first light, the couple sent for the parish priest, who recovered the Host—by then, tradition holds, transformed into what witnesses described as living flesh and blood.
He returned it to the church, where the bleeding reportedly continued for three more days before the relic was sealed inside a beeswax reliquary.

A further sign is recorded from 1340, when a priest opening the tabernacle found the wax container shattered and the relic enclosed instead within a vessel of crystal, where it has remained ever since.
Legacy

Several popes, including St. Pius V, later granted plenary indulgences to pilgrims visiting the relic, which remains enshrined today in what is now called the Church of the Holy Miracle in Santarém, not far from the shrine at Fátima .
Each year, on the second Sunday of April, it is carried in procession from the house where the events are said to have taken place to the church.
By its own account, the city has kept this devotion since the Middle Ages.
